rows.en: God watches over man, the choicest of creatures, and His eyes run to and fro through the whole earth (Zechariah 4; 2 Chronicles 15⚠1). Divine providence extends over all the details of deeds, and the events of the world, in general and in particular, are in the hand of God, and nothing is in the will of man except the fear of Heaven (*Antiquities* 13); and it is an ancient proverb: everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven. The saying "All is foreseen, and freedom is given" (Avot 3), which is attributed to R. Akiva, was not invented by him; it was a foundation of the faith of Israel from of old. They did not enter into speculations to reconcile the concept of foreseeing, or divine knowledge, with the concept of freedom, which contradict each other. Rather, both were established beliefs, and they did not question them. Therefore they believed that man has free will and that there is no decree of God upon him to do evil or to do good (Ben Sira 15:20); and they believed that the deeds of man are revealed before the Lord before they are done (ibid. ch. 23 and in many places); and they believed in divine decree (*Antiquities* 13) — in agreement with the Essenes — that a man does not hurt his finger below unless it is proclaimed concerning him above (Ḥullin 7b); and they believed that the inclination to evil was planted in the heart of the first man (4 Ezra 4:30), and this is the root of the aggadah about the filth that the serpent cast into Eve, which clings to human beings (Shabbat 146a); and they believed that Satan acts upon the will of man and incites him (1 Chronicles 21). Satan is also described so in the prophecy of Zechariah (3:1), and with a small departure from what is described in Job, where Satan acts as the messenger of the Lord. But the later [writers] describe Satan as inciting: he goes down and leads astray (Bava Batra 15a⚠2), as in Zechariah and Chronicles, and he goes up and accuses, as described in Job. Satan is the evil inclination, and he is the angel of death (ibid.); and this is founded on the belief that the sin of the first man, through the counsel of the serpent, brought death upon the generations. These beliefs — in providence, in divine knowledge, in the freedom of man, and in the inclination to sin — contradict each other, and yet they stood firm in the nation, for they were believers, sons of believers, and did not enter into speculations. The Lord who watches is the King of the world, and His kingship is called the kingdom of Heaven. He rules over the nations as over Israel, but upon Israel His name rests most of all (Sifre Va-etḥannan, sec. 31). To the peoples He allotted kings of flesh and blood, but upon Israel He set the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven (Ben Sira 17:13). This belief was strengthened by the Zealots, who led the revolt before the destruction, and who fixed it firmly (*Antiquities* 17; Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 20). All the peoples are His, but He has placed them under the charge of His angels, while over Israel He Himself rules and watches (*Book of Jubilees* ch. 15; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer ch. 24). Out of His love for Israel He made known to the nations that He Himself guides them, so that they would treat them with honor (Mekhilta Be-shallaḥ ch. 1). To set apart the deity of the one Lord, as if He were only the God of the Jews and not the God of the nations, was not among the foundations of their faith; rather, they believed that the Lord saves all who come into the world, and Israel more, because of their righteousness and their faith (ibid. ch. 3). God glories in Israel because He too is the glory of their strength (ג"ו⚠3 ibid.). He makes them one unique entity in the world because they too made Him one unique entity in the world (Ḥagigah 3a; Ben Sira in many places; Psalms of Solomon⚠4 ch. 2, 3, 10). And therefore Israel are beloved and are called children of the Omnipresent (Avot 3 and in many places), and He deals with His children by the measure of mercy (Berakhot 7a) and inclines their judgment toward lovingkindness (Rosh Hashanah 17a). Even if the judgment has been decreed, it is in the power of man to annul it through charity, prayer and repentance (Rosh Hashanah 16b; Yerushalmi Ta'anit 2; Tobit 12); for one who does charity is like one who offers a sacrifice (Ben Sira 35), and it is reckoned as a ransom and redemption of the soul (Daniel 4:24). Likewise prayer is service of the heart and is esteemed like the service of the altar (Sifre Ekev, sec. 81⚠5), and the Holy One, blessed be He, longs for it (Yevamot 94a⚠6), when one prays in purity of heart and with gravity (Berakhot 5:1), and with mercy and supplication before the Omnipresent (Avot 2); and then the Holy One, blessed be He, annuls His decree because of the decree of the righteous man (Yerushalmi Ta'anit 3:12). Likewise repentance atones (Mekhilta Ba-ḥodesh ch. 6; Bavli and Yerushalmi Yoma ch. 8; and in many places), and the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, is stretched out to receive penitents (Pesaḥim 119a), on condition that the repentance is complete; for one who says "I will repent and sin [again]" is like one who immerses with a creeping thing in his hand (Ben Sira 34; Yoma 86a).

2.note: The saying on Satan (goes down and leads astray, goes up and accuses) is Bava Batra 16a; the print reads ט"ו.

4.note: Read as Psalms of Solomon, as in the other references of this section.

5.note: 'Service of the heart' is in Sifre Ekev, sec. 41; the print has פ"א (81).

6.note: 'The Holy One longs for the prayer of the righteous' is Yevamot 64a; the print has צ"ד.

rows.en: The princes of the kingdom of Heaven are the ministering angels. The names of the angels came up with them from Babylon (Yerushalmi Rosh Hashanah 1:1), and therefore they are not mentioned by their names in the early Holy Scriptures, but only in the late ones (Daniel 8, 10). There they are called princes, and every kingdom of the kingdoms of the earth has a prince. Michael is the prince of Israel (ibid. 10:21), and he is one of the chief princes (ibid. 10:13). Seven princes of the Presence are mentioned (Tobit 12), corresponding to the seven princes of the Persians, who are called Amshaspands. The angels of the Presence are a special kind (*Book of Jubilees* ch. 2), and they are Metatron, prince of the Presence (Sanhedrin 38b), and Suriel, prince of the Presence (Berakhot 51a). There are also angels of holiness (*Book of Jubilees*, ibid.), and they are called holy ones (Daniel 4:14) and also watchers (Daniel; *Jubilees*, ibid.; and the *Book of Enoch*). Gabriel is distinguished by the name "holy one" (Daniel 8:13); he is counted in the company of Michael, Raphael (Bava Metzia 86b), Uriel, Suriel and Penuel (*Book of Enoch* ch. 9). The greatest of them all is Michael (Yoma 37a). Gabriel is also called Ruaḥ Pisqonit, and he has three names: Pisqon, Itmon, Sigron (Sanhedrin 44a). To all the phenomena of nature they gave princes, spirits and angels (*Book of Enoch* ch. 55). Rahab is the prince of the sea (Bava Batra 74b); Dumah is the angel of the spirits (ibid. 94b); Yurkemo is the prince of hail (Pesaḥim 118a); Lailah is the angel of conception (Niddah 15b). There were also angels who pray on behalf of man; one of them is Sandalfon (Ḥagigah 13b). Metatron writes the deeds of men in a book (ibid. 15a), and he is Enoch son of Jared, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, hid away (Yalkut Isaiah, sec. 315). For all this there are parallels in the *Book of Enoch* and *Jubilees*. Besides the princes appointed over natural matters there are seventy princes, one prince for each people, and angels and evil spirits without end. And they said: "Were the eye given leave to see, no creature could stand before the demons" (Berakhot 6a; Philo, in the book *On Dreams*, 636⚠1). Every derangement of the mind they ascribed to an evil spirit (*Antiquities* 6:8). Samael is the inciter and Satan (Sotah 10b). Azael, one of the angels who came down to earth, also incites to transgression (Yalkut, ibid. 44; Yoma 66b). One kind of the evil spirits are the demons. In their existence they believed with all their heart, so that they became the cause for the foundation of a number of laws and rules (Shabbat 2:5; Gittin 66a; Yevamot 122a; Sanhedrin 44a). They are also mentioned by name, such as Ashmedai, the prince of them all (Gittin 68a); Lilith, a demon that has wings (Niddah 24a) and is the prince of the night (Shabbat 152b); Hurmiz son of Lilith (Bava Batra 73a); and Ben Temalion (Me'ilah 17b). They said that there were three hundred kinds of demons in Shiḥin (Gittin 68b). One kind of evil spirits is called angels of destruction, and their number is great (Shabbat 88a; Pesaḥim 112b), and they too are designated by names. The mouth cannot tell the multitude of inventions that the imagination devised in these matters, and all of them found believers.

1.note: The first sign of the figure is unclear in the print; read as 636, probably a page of Mangey's edition of Philo.

rows.en: The angels reveal themselves to the righteous. Elijah the prophet, who is in the rank of an angel, goes about from city to city (Bava Kamma 60b), guards the ways of men, makes known the secret of the Lord to those who fear Him (Berakhot 3a), and resolves their doubts (Pesaḥim 70a). The righteousness of the righteous man can bring him to the holy spirit. Although the holy spirit ceased with the prophets (end of Sotah, Bavli and Yerushalmi), nevertheless they believed that the holy spirit was revealed by chance to individuals, or that they heard a heavenly voice (ibid. 33a; מ"ת⚠1 ch. 11; Sanhedrin 11a; and in many places). And since the righteous are near to God, they believed that they could do good to others through the prayer that they pray for them; and in every time of trouble they sent to the famous righteous men to pray on behalf of the people (Berakhot 34b; Ta'anit ch. 2, Bavli and Yerushalmi). Likewise they believed that it was in the power of the righteous to act by means of whispered charms. For we have seen that in the last years of the Temple this was a craft for some of them, who boasted of this power; and this was not a new invention, but such was the belief among the people, and therefore they opposed with all their strength those who whisper over a wound (Sanhedrin 10:1). Ben Dama, the son of R. Ishmael's sister, wanted to be healed by Jacob of Kefar Sekhaniah in the name of his master (Yerushalmi Avodah Zarah 2, and the Bavli there, and Tosefta Ḥullin 2). Without doubt the matter of the whispered charms was the use of the names of the Holy One, blessed be He, and adjurations, which they made in a whisper; and the charms are already hinted at in the early Holy Scriptures. They also believed that there was power to act by whispering the names of impurity (Sanhedrin 91a), and these are the names of the demons, and especially the name of Satan; whisperings by the name of Satan and sorcery are one and the same. The belief in sorcery is old in the nation. The women were given over to sorcery (Avot 2:5⚠2; Eruvin 64b), and in the days of Simeon ben Shetaḥ it was the sickness of the time (Sanhedrin 45b); and from ancient days sorcery was the craft of women, for the Torah itself speaks of a sorceress [Exodus 22:17]. The aggadah relates that the angels who came to the daughters of men taught them sorcery and adjurations (*Book of Enoch* 7:10, and Yalkut, sec. 44). Yet the practice of sorcery was an abomination in their eyes, and although they believed in its effect, nevertheless those who practised it were persecuted. But the adjurations and charms — to remove illnesses by a charm, and evil spirits by adjurations — even the enlightened did not oppose those who practised them, since they believed in them with complete faith. They ascribed the scrolls of adjurations and charms to King Solomon (*Antiquities* 8:2). All these were reckoned as channels that join the spiritual world with the material world. One special channel among them was the dream. The enlightened of the people endeavoured to teach that there is nothing in dreams and that they come only "through much business" (Ecclesiastes 5:2); visions of the night are vain images (ibid. 5:6; Ben Sira 34), and we should not fear them, but only fear God (ibid.). But they were of no avail against the belief of the people, which was very strong; and it was almost a special craft in Jerusalem to interpret dreams (Berakhot 55a). These opinions, which spread in those days, frightened them at every single step of their way, so that they were afraid to utter a bad word from their mouths, lest they bring Satan upon them (Berakhot 19a). This became a principle: "A man should not open his mouth to Satan." When they spoke of an evil that would come upon Israel, they said "upon the enemies of Israel," out of fear lest they arouse Satan by their speech. And they believed in omens for good or for evil (Berakhot 34b). For many generations more they could not separate themselves from divinations (Ḥullin 95b) and from signs and portents (Mekhilta Bo ch. 1; Sukkah 29a), but the greatest of the sages fought them with all their might (Shabbat 66a; Sanhedrin 65b; and Mekhilta, ibid.). It is indeed so that not all these opinions are rational and in agreement with the opinions of the Torah and the Prophets; but their source is pure, for all of them were hewn from the belief in divine providence. As one mother bears sons who differ from one another in appearance, in stature and in beauty, so from this belief came forth different offspring: some of them good and healthy, and some of them thin and of evil spirit; but in all of them a little of the spirit of their mother still clings.

1.note: Abbreviation unclear (perhaps Megillat Ta'anit or Midrash Tannaim); kept as printed.

2.note: 'More women, more sorcery' is Avot 2:7; reference kept as printed.

rows.en: The choicest offspring that came forth from the belief in providence is the belief in reward and punishment. Their belief was firm that everything that comes to a man, of good or of evil, in temporal life is the outcome of his deeds and their fruits (Pe'ah 1; Menaḥot 44a). Whether for good or for evil, the Holy One, blessed be He, repays measure for measure (Sotah 8b and in many places); but the measure of good is greater than the measure of punishment (Sanhedrin 100a and in many places; Ben Sira 35). If evil comes upon the righteous, it is for a trial or for atonement, and so that their reward may be complete in the world to come (Ben Sira 2; Tobit 2; Psalms of Solomon in many places; Ta'anit 11a; Bava Batra 15b; Horayot 10b); and He does good to the wicked man in this world in order to drive him out of the world to come (Bava Batra, ibid.; Sifre Ha'azinu, sec. 306). Sometimes the righteous die for the sin of the generation, so that they should not learn from the deeds of the generation (Psalms of Solomon ch. 4, and in the Gemara in many places), or to atone for their generation (Sifre Ve-zot ha-Berakhah, sec. 344), or because of the punishment that is ready to come (Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 15). Good comes to Israel by the merit of the fathers, and the Holy One, blessed be He, remembers for the children the kindnesses of their fathers and the wickedness of their fathers. Ezekiel (18) already decided that this holds only when they hold the deeds of their fathers in their hands; and this was a principle for them at all times (Ben Sira in many places; Sanhedrin 27b). A reward is also appointed after death. When a man dies his soul does not perish; rather, it remains for eternal life. The souls of the righteous are placed in a treasury (Sifre Pinḥas 139; Ve-zot ha-Berakhah 344) and are stored away beneath the Throne of Glory (Ḥagigah 12b). When a man dies there are two ways before him, one to the Garden of Eden and one to Gehinnom (Berakhot 28b), and he gives account of his deeds before God (Avot 3). Of the nature of the reward and the punishment they spoke only by hint. In the book of 4 Ezra the matters are precise to a hair's breadth (ch. 6), and in a number of things there is agreement between it and the books of the Oral Torah. For example: the righteous are placed in a treasury where the eternal light is (Genesis Rabbah 3); the souls of the wicked are handed over to angels of destruction (Sifre Ve-zot ha-Berakhah 357), and these angels come to meet them and receive them, while the righteous are received by the ministering angels (Ketubbot 104a); the righteous enjoy the radiance of the Shekhinah (Berakhot 17a); the deeds of man, written in a book (Avot 3), are spelled out before him, and he is judged for them and acknowledges the justice of the judgment (Sifre Ha'azinu 306; Ta'anit 11a); and there are seven grades for the righteous in the Garden of Eden (Sifre Deuteronomy 10). For all these there are parallels in 4 Ezra. These images lived in the belief of the people, and the imagination invented a thousand like them; but the basis of the matter was agreed by all: that the soul does not wither after death. Ecclesiastes, with his doubts in the reckoning of the soul after death (9:10), decides that the spirit returns to God (12:7). In most of the Apocrypha the belief in the survival of the soul is mentioned, either by hint (Ben Sira 45:20 and 48:5, 15) or explicitly (Tobit 2:18; Psalms of Solomon in many places; 2 Maccabees ch. 11). The concept of the survival of the soul is described in terms of the storing away of the soul, because they believed that the souls are kept for the last day of judgment (Psalms of Solomon in many places; Enoch; Ezra; Jubilees; *Antiquities* 18; Sanhedrin 108a). The souls of the wicked are bound and kept in Sheol (Enoch, Ezra and Jubilees), and they have no permission to return among the living; but the righteous have permission to return (*Antiquities*, ibid.; Berakhot 18b), and therefore they called the righteous "living" even in their death (Yerushalmi, ibid. 2:8; Matthew 22:32). Of the belief in the transmigration of souls there is no hint in the books of the Oral Torah, but in other books of the ancient Jews hints are found. According to the testimony of Josephus (*Wars* 2:8), they believed that the souls of the righteous come into another body. 4 Ezra (ch. 6) asks whether the souls will be revealed in new bodies, and this is a sign that in the days of the writer they believed so. Also in the writings of the Evangelists (Matthew 14:2) there is some hint; but one cannot decide clearly that this belief was widespread among the people.

The chief reward and punishment is on the last day of judgment, before whose coming the Messiah will be revealed. The belief in the coming of the Messiah took root in the nation from of old (above, ch. 3). From the time that the Temple was destroyed the first time, it branched out further with the opinions of the people. As the troubles grew, the hope for redemption also grew stronger. In its root this hope was shared by the whole nation, but the description of its outward form was not shared by all. For the images of the character of the redeemer changed according to the political situation, according to the abundance or scarcity of their troubles, and according to the level of enlightenment. Just as the earlier prophets differed from the later ones in their images of the Messiah, so that the stamp of each time is seen impressed upon them, so it was in the days of the Second Temple. In the days of their going up from the exile their sun shone and salvation was near; then, when their heart still sought, they held fast⚠1 in their hope to the completeness of the redemption. Nehemiah hopes that a priest will stand up with Urim and Thummim (Ezra 3:66⚠2), and that the Lord will bring them to the place that He chose and gather the dispersed of Israel (Nehemiah 1:9). One of the prophets of the exile (Isaiah II), who prophesied in the days of Cyrus, hopes for a complete redemption and an everlasting salvation: for the ingathering of the exiles and for the payment of recompense to the enemies of the Lord, so that they may fear Him; the light of the Lord will shine upon Israel, and the nations will walk by its light, and all will see the glory of the Lord, and, like Israel, will bring an offering to His house in Jerusalem; and then the wolf and the lamb will feed together, and there will be no destroyer in all His holy mountain, and the wicked who turned away from the Lord will be judged and go to perdition, and they will be an abhorrence to all flesh. Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi also described the redemption in this way. At the end of the prophecies of Malachi a new matter is found: that the Lord sends them Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great day of the Lord [Malachi 3:23]. But he concealed from us what that great day is: is it the coming of the Messiah or the last day of judgment? Is he the herald of the coming of the Messiah, or is he himself the redeemer? But I have already shown above that these last verses in Malachi are not part of the book, but were appended to serve as the seal of the collection of the Torah and the Prophets; and that the name "Elijah the prophet" does not refer to the ancient Elijah, but refers to prophecy in general: that God will return and raise up a prophet for them as at first (see above, end of ch. 3, in the note). None of them speaks of the coming of the son of David. In the book of Baruch (chs. 4, 5) he describes the redemption as the ingathering of the exiles, temporal and moral happiness, and the subjugation of their enemies. So too it is described in the book of Tobit, and it adds further (ch. 13) that nations will gather to the Temple of the Lord in Jerusalem and serve the God of Israel, and forsake their idols and rejoice with Israel (ch. 14), and the kingdom of the Almighty will rise over them forever (end of ch. 13). From the writings of the Alexandrian Jews too (2 Maccabees 1:34–36 and 2:18, 19) these longings and hopes sparkle. Ben Sira (ch. 36) also speaks of the punishment of the nations, so that they may know the Lord as Israel His people, and he desires that the Lord raise up prophets for them as of old; and in all other matters his hopes do not deviate from the opinions of the prophets and writers mentioned. One cannot believe that it is only by chance that the establishing⚠3 of the kingdom of the house of David is not mentioned even in a single word; and likewise one cannot believe that they did not hope that the kingdom of David would return as of old. But their political situation forced them, in all those times, not to reveal the secrets of their heart, for the sake of the peace of the government. This is seen also in the writings of Josephus. Is not the subject of all his books the history of the Jews, their religion and their faith? Yet there is not a word in his speech about their hope for the coming of the Messiah and for the restoration of the kingdom of the house of David. This can only be because of his wish to keep the peace with the Romans, for whom especially his books were intended. In the book of Daniel the teaching of the Messiah is found more explicit and more extended than in all the late writings that were written up to the end of the days of the Maccabees. This book was attributed to Daniel, who was one of the exiles and famous for his righteousness (Ezekiel 14) and became a byword for his wisdom (ibid. 28); a man wise and righteous like him was the fitting man to whom the prophecies written in the book could be attributed. But in truth it was composed in the days of the persecution of the Jews by Antiochus Epiphanes; and therefore all the events in the days of the Persian rule are coloured with legendary images, and some of them are contradicted by the facts, whereas all its reports of the events in the days of the Greek kings agree with what happened to a hair. Speaking in all innocence, the book itself testifies to its own time, when it says that he was commanded to shut up the vision for many days (8:26⚠4) and to seal the book until the time of the end (12:4). Is this not as though it excuses itself for why it was not known in former times, through all the days of the Persians and the first Greek kings, and did not come to light until the time of the end, and says that so Daniel was commanded? Indeed, for us today this is clear testimony that the beginning of its coming to light, which was in the days of the persecutions, is also the time of its composition.{v1_12_11:1} And it is clear that there was no memory of these prophecies before that time; for otherwise, why did Ben Sira not mention Daniel among the men of wonder and the prophets, to all of whom he gave a memorial? Now if we consider the book where it speaks of the Messiah, we find that in the essence of the matter it did not depart from the opinions in the other writings of that time; only it describes explicitly what others said only by hint. The first image it gives is in the dream of Nebuchadnezzar. In his dream, behold, a great image: its head of gold, its breast and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, its legs of iron, and the feet partly of iron and partly of clay. Then a stone was cut out not by hands, and it smashed the feet of the image, and the stone became a great mountain that filled the whole earth. These parts of the image are four kingdoms (Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece), and the stone that smashes the fourth kingdom is the kingdom of Israel. At that time the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the sovereignty be left to another people; it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever (2:44, 45). And Daniel sees in a dream of the night four beasts coming up from the sea, the fourth very terrible, and its mouth speaking great things; and the Ancient of Days sits upon a throne, and the fourth beast is given over to destruction in a stream of fire, and from the other beasts too the kingdom is taken away. And behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man; he reached the Ancient of Days, and to him were given dominion and glory and kingdom, and all the nations and tongues shall bow down to him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed (4:13, 14⚠5). And Daniel receives the interpretation from the angel: the four beasts are four kingdoms (Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece), all of which will perish; and the one like a son of man is the people of the saints of the Most High, to whom the kingdom under all the heavens is given, which will be an everlasting kingdom, and all the rulers shall obey them and bow down to them (7:26). Now just as the beasts are images of four kingdoms, so the likeness of a son of man is an image of Israel; and therefore "son of man" does not refer to a Messiah, but to the kingdom of Israel, and that is the kingdom of the Messiah. In these two visions it is not said who will be the means of attaining world dominion; it is only said that the Lord will set up the kingdom, and not through whom. But in the prophecies in the Hebrew part of the book the end of the four kingdoms and the history of the fourth are told in great detail, and with wonderful art every point of the annals of Antiochus the wicked is described in its bearing on the Jews. And there shall be a time of trouble for Israel such as never was, and at that time Michael the great prince shall stand up for Israel, and at that time they shall be delivered according to all{v1_12_12:1} that is found written in the book (12:1). This refers to the fulfilment of the prophecies written in the Aramaic part, which he called "the book": that God will set up the kingdom of Israel over all the earth, and after He sets this up, then the resurrection of the dead will take place. From this it is seen that the images of the kingdom of the Messiah in the book of Daniel are the images that all the writers of his time held: the eternity of the nation, the spreading of its kingdom over all the peoples, and its endurance for ever and ever. Who will be the king in this kingdom? Of this the book is silent. Perhaps the matter was understood of itself: if we speak of an enduring kingdom in Israel, its king will be of the house of David. Therefore in the days of the book of Daniel the teaching of the Messiah did not reach a new stage; but those who studied the book and its expounders who came after it gave its words an intention other than what the writer intended, and this gave birth to new opinions on the matter of the Messiah and his kingdom.

2.note: The priest with Urim and Thummim is Ezra 2:63 (Nehemiah 7:65); kept as printed.

3.note: Read as הכנת ('establishing'); the sense may be 'restoration'.

4.note: ה or ח unclear in the print; Daniel 8:26 is the verse meant.

5.note: The vision of the one like a son of man is Daniel 7:13-14; kept as printed.

footnotes.en: See R. N. Krochmal's *Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 11, and the introductions to Holy Scripture, and the recent commentators on Daniel, who have brought still further proofs.
